Why it helps validity/security: Assesses both final product and how the learner arrived there.
Example implementation: Require draft history, feedback use, revision memo, and final artifact.
Caution: Do not overvalue busywork; define representative evidence.

Why it helps validity/security: Probes reasoning, assumptions, and transfer beyond a submitted artifact.
Works best for: High-stakes work, projects, models, code, writing
Example implementation: Two to five structured questions after submission.
Caution: Needs rubrics/common prompts to maintain fairness.

Why it helps validity/security: Provides direct evidence of skills that cannot be represented fully in text.
Works best for: Clinical, lab, teaching, performance, technical skills

Why it helps validity/security: Constrains task to evidence the learner gathered or a local context AI cannot infer.
Example implementation: Use campus/community observations, unique datasets, field notes.
Caution: Protect privacy and avoid burdensome access requirements.

Why it helps validity/security: Changing information requires situated decision-making rather than static text generation.
Example implementation: Release case updates and ask learners to revise decisions.
Caution: Avoid unnecessary complexity; align updates to outcomes.

Why it helps validity/security: Develops evaluative judgment and provides additional evidence of criteria use.
Example implementation: Peer review with calibration against exemplars.
Caution: Train students on criteria; do not rely solely on peer grades.

Why it helps validity/security: Forces adaptation of communication, evidence, and recommendations to context.
Example implementation: Briefing for a role-specific stakeholder with Q&A.
Caution: Avoid simulated authenticity that adds irrelevant barriers.

Why it helps validity/security: Assesses responsible tool use instead of pretending AI was not available.
Example implementation: Prompt log, AI output, verification sources, human edits, decision rationale.
Caution: Only use when policy permits AI; be clear about allowed/prohibited uses.

Why it helps validity/security: Improves consistency when assessing complex performance evidence.
Example implementation: Analytic rubric, anchor examples, norming discussion.
Caution: Rubrics do not guarantee validity by themselves; align to outcome.

Why it helps validity/security: Separates collaboration evidence from individual learning evidence.
Example implementation: Contribution statements, peer evaluation, individual oral questions.
Caution: Avoid punitive peer ratings; use multiple evidence sources.

Why it helps validity/security: Forces the assessment to rely on highly recent, proprietary, or geographically constrained parameters that bypass general LLM training data or pre-programmed knowledge cutoffs.
Works best for: Reports, Policy Briefs, Case Studies, Social Sciences, Educational Leadership
Example implementation: Analyzing a niche community dispute or a brand-new local school board policy using firsthand stakeholder interviews or local meeting notes.
Caution: Can introduce equity disparities if some students lack equal physical access to local sites or niche resources.

Why it helps validity/security: Shifts evaluation from the final polished document to the chronological evolution of the work, rendering "one-shot" AI text generation completely visible and inadequate.
Works best for: Computer Science (Code Repositories), Long-form Essays, Capstones, Research Plans
Example implementation: Requiring students to submit interactive version-tracked drafts (e.g., git commit history logs) detailing explicit revisions made in response to milestones.
Caution: Markedly increases the grading and tracking workload for instructors monitoring multiple touchpoints.

Why it helps validity/security: Validates genuine intellectual ownership and conversational agility through unscripted, spontaneous verbal explanation, instantly peeling away superficial AI fluency.
Works best for: Presentations, Group Projects, Business Pitches, Senior Capstones
Example implementation: Implementing a brief 3-to-5 minute synchronous Q&A session post-submission where students must verbally defend specific technical design choices.
Caution: Highly time-prohibitive in large classes and can inadvertently penalize non-native speakers or induce severe anxiety.

Why it helps validity/security: Moves higher-order evaluation to the forefront by framing a flawed AI-generated artifact as the direct object of critique, targeting student discernment instead of text production.
Works best for: Code Reviews, Fact-Checking Exercises, Literature Summaries, Answer Questions
Example implementation: Supplying students with a highly fluent but factually hollow AI synthesis of a reading and requiring them to cross-verify and annotate its omissions.
Caution: Demands a high level of baseline AI and data literacy from both the students and the instructional staff to grade fairly.

Why it helps validity/security: Anchors the conceptual and analytical output to un-scrapable, student-generated raw datasets collected in a specific time and environment.
Works best for: Lab Reports, Physical Science Experiments, Observational Logs
Example implementation: Building a quantitative analysis model entirely dependent on unique data parameters measured by the student during a live lab or site visit.
Caution: Highly dependent on successful data collection; if a student's data collection fails, the entire assessment pipeline breaks down.
